# Business-Model Transition: Perpetual Licence to Subscription
## Offer Architecture, Migration Economics, Sales and Channel Compensation, Trough Governance

**Version 2.0 — complete for decision.** For the Board.
Circulated in advance to: CEO; CFO; **Treasurer**; Chief Revenue Officer; Chief Product Officer; **Chief Customer Officer / Head of Renewals**; General Counsel; Chief Accounting Officer; **CIO / Head of Business Systems (billing, CPQ, entitlement)**; VP Investor Relations; Head of Partner & Channel; **Chair, Compensation Committee**; **Chair, Audit Committee**.
Not yet for customer, employee, partner, analyst or market communication (§12.6, §14).

*Prior to Board circulation, the substance of §§6, 9 and 10 has been walked through individually with the CRO, the Head of Partner & Channel and the Chief Customer Officer, and the substance of §§4 and 11 with the CAO and Treasurer. Where their views differ from ours, we have recorded the difference rather than resolved it (§16.3). We would not wish the Board to discover a disagreement in the room that could have been surfaced on paper.*

---

### How to read this pack

Four notes, then the substance.

**On what this is not.** This is not a pricing exercise with a communications annexe attached. The documented failure pattern in this category is a company that redesigns its price book while leaving its compensation plan, its billing stack, its board scorecard and its investor narrative on the old model — and discovers six quarters later that every part of the organisation is still paid, measured and praised for selling the thing it has publicly stopped selling. Nor is it a request for more time. The direction has been decided by leadership [F]; our task is to specify it. Every design choice below is **named**; only the calibration is pending, and §15 says precisely which data sets it.

**On numbers, and on the existing model.** We have been shown leadership's transition model, which projects a multi-year revenue trough [F]. We regard it as soundly constructed and we have not rebuilt it. We would, respectfully, test six of its inputs (§3); on three we think the model is likely to be wrong, and we say in which direction. Beyond that model, illustrative values are used solely to show how the arithmetic behaves and are marked *[illus.]*. They carry no evidential weight and should not be quoted outside this room. Where a figure matters to a decision requested in §16, it appears in §15 with a named owner and a delivery date.

**On sequencing.** There is a natural instinct to defer the irreversible decisions until the reversible ones have been proved. It is a reasonable instinct and it is, we think, the trap. The longest-lead items — billing and entitlement systems, the auditor's revenue-recognition position, debt covenants, and the Board's own incentive metrics — are exactly the ones that feel least urgent and take longest to move. They sit in **Phase 0** (§11) for that reason. *A transition announced before its plumbing exists announces its own failure on a nine-month delay.*

**On consultation.** Two of the four constituencies affected by this plan — the field sales organisation and the long-standing installed base — will experience it as something being taken away. Our strong view is that neither should learn the shape of it from a company-wide announcement. §9.7 and §6.7 set out a deliberate sequence of small-group soundings, advisory-council testing and named-sponsor conversations *before* publication. This adds roughly five weeks to the calendar. We think it is the cheapest insurance in the pack, and it is the principal difference between our plan and what the comparator appears to have done (§2).

**Evidence markers.**
**[F]** fact stated in the brief. **[M]** figure or assumption drawn from leadership's existing transition model. **[P]** publicly documented comparator transition — directional only, to be verified by IR before any external use. **[A]** assumption, pending the data in §15. **[J]** our judgement, argued in the text and open to challenge.

---

## 1. Recommendation on a page

**Adopt a three-year "Balanced" transition. Do not force conversion; make staying more expensive than moving, slowly and predictably. Use an on-premise term licence as the deliberate trough-shaping instrument, not as a compromise. Price the entry conversion at parity with today's maintenance and buy the customer's consent with a three-year price-certainty window and a capped uplift thereafter. Pay the sales force on total contracted value with a declining transition multiplier and four quarters of protected earnings, and replace the channel's upfront margin before, not after, partners discover it has gone. Move the plumbing, the auditor position, the covenants and the Board's own comp metrics in Phase 0. Then pre-publish the trough — floor quarter, depth and recovery quarter — and be judged against a scorecard we choose, disclose and never quietly change.**

| | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| **Direction** | Subscription-first, but **not SaaS-only**. Three deployment forms sold from one price book: Cloud (ratable), **Term Licence on-premise** (partially recognised at delivery), Perpetual (closed to new customers at Month 12; available to existing base only by exception until Month 24) (§4, §5) |
| **The single largest trough lever** | Revenue recognition, treated as a **design variable, not plumbing.** Directing an [illus.] 35–45% of on-premise subscription bookings to term licence rather than hosted can materially reduce reported-revenue trough depth while building the same recurring commitment (§4.3) [J][A] |
| **Offer tiers** | Three editions — **Essential / Professional / Enterprise** — replacing the perpetual-plus-maintenance SKU sprawl. Enterprise carries the entitlements the top decile actually buys support for (§5.2) |
| **Headline price ratio** | Like-for-like Cloud subscription at **1.30–1.45 × current annual maintenance** for *new* customers; **1.00 × current maintenance for the first three years** for existing licence holders who convert in the Early Window (§6.2, §7.2) *[illus., calibrated by §15 items 3, 5, 9]* |
| **Migration ladder** | Four rungs, price rising and terms tightening at each: **Early Window (Months 1–12) → Standard Window (13–24) → Late Window (25–36) → Support Sunset.** No retrospective removal of perpetual rights, ever (§6) |
| **Trade-in credit** | Residual-value credit on the customer's declining unamortised licence value, applied against first-year subscription, capped and expiring with the Early Window (§6.3) |
| **The entitlement principle, stated plainly** | Perpetual licences are irrevocable property and we will say so publicly and without qualification. **Support, updates and cloud services are renewable and, with notice, sunsettable.** That distinction is the whole of the migration economics and must be handled as a relationship matter before it is a contract matter (§6.1) |
| **Support sunset** | Announced at Month 0, effective **Month 36** for new-version entitlement and **Month 48** for security-only support, with a priced Extended Support tier at 1.5× legacy maintenance for those who genuinely cannot move. Contractual notice periods verified per-contract by GC before announcement (§6.5) |
| **Sales compensation** | **TCV crediting with a transition multiplier declining 1.6× → 1.3× → 1.0× over three years**; ratable quota retirement; **four quarters of protected earnings at 90% of trailing-eight-quarter average**; migration-specific SPIFF; 12-month churn clawback; quota and territory reset published only after the soundings in §9.7 (§9) |
| **Channel** | Upfront VAR margin is structurally destroyed by subscription and partners will resist accordingly [J]. Replace with a **front-loaded first-year margin (higher than the old licence margin in year 1), a declining renewal annuity margin, a migration bounty per converted seat, and deal-registration protection extended to renewals** (§10) |
| **Trough shape, recommended scenario** | Balanced: revenue trough floor in **Q6–Q7**, depth **[illus.] 11–14%** below the Month-0 run-rate, recovery to prior peak by **Q11–Q13**; cash trough shallower and earlier than the revenue trough because of annual-upfront billing (§7.4, §8) [M][A] |
| **The two troughs** | **Revenue trough and cash trough are different animals with different remedies.** Cash is managed with annual-upfront billing as default, multi-year prepay discounts, and RPO build; revenue is managed with mix (term licence) and pace. Investors discount them differently and we will disclose them separately (§8) |
| **Investor architecture** | Metric switch to **ARR, cRPO, gross and net retention, cohort conversion rate, billings**; guidance **re-based to a three-year framework, not suspended**; trough floor and recovery quarter **pre-committed and published**; Analyst Day at Month 3 with cohort disclosure; covenant amendment **completed before announcement**; buyback used as a floor, not a rescue (§12) |
| **Board's own metrics** | The Compensation Committee must re-cut executive metrics **before** the announcement. We are otherwise asking the executive team to depress, deliberately and for three years, the numbers on which it is paid. This is a Phase 0 item, not a year-end item (§11.5) |
| **Governance** | **Dual operating model.** Perpetual run-off and subscription new business managed, forecast and reported separately, with a named **Transition Office** lead reporting to the CEO and dotted to the CFO, appointed within 15 days. The CRO cannot both hit this year's licence number and dismantle it [J] (§13) |
| **Adjust triggers, not abort triggers** | We do not recommend an abort trigger; a publicly reversed transition is worse than either state. We recommend **three pace-adjustment triggers** on gross retention, top-decile conversion and cash (§14.3) |
| **Decisions requested** | **Six**, listed in §16, sought at the Board meeting on **[date]** |

### 1.1 Our posture, said once and plainly

Two things deserve saying before the detail.

First: **the comparator's loss of a fifth of its installed base is the most valuable piece of information we have** [F], and it is the design constraint for everything that follows. Our reading — offered for testing, not for adoption — is that abrupt transitions do not fail on price. They fail because **optionality is withdrawn without notice**, which converts a pricing conversation into a dignity conversation, and dignity conversations are lost by vendors. A customer who is told "your choice is gone" will look at competitors, third-party support providers and version-freeze even when the economics of staying are better. §2 sets out how to size this before we design against it.

Second: **20% base loss is not automatically a failure, and 0% base loss is not automatically a success.** The relevant test is asymmetric (§2.3). Losing a fifth of the *seat* count at a materially higher revenue per retained customer may be value-accretive. Losing a fifth of the *top decile* — the reference customers, the multi-site accounts, the ones whose logos carry the analyst narrative — is not recoverable in this decade. We therefore recommend that the plan be tuned to protect the top decile almost regardless of cost, and be considerably more relaxed about the long tail, where a partner-led or self-serve motion may serve better than we do.

We would also ask that the transition be described internally, consistently and from the first day, as something the company is doing **with** its customers and its sales force rather than **to** them. If people believe otherwise, we will spend the trough managing defections rather than conversions, and the pace-adjustment triggers in §14.3 will all fire at once.

---

## 2. The comparator's 20%: decomposition before design

### 2.1 What we need to know, and how to know it

We should not design against a headline. Before the Month-3 gate we should decompose the comparator's loss from public sources and channel intelligence [P], accepting that the picture will be partial.

| Question | Why it changes our design |
|---|---|
| **Which segments left?** Small/tail, mid-market, or enterprise? | If tail-heavy, our tail can be moved to a partner-led motion and our own risk is lower than the headline. If enterprise-heavy, the Early Window incentives in §6.2 must be materially richer |
| **What ARR left, versus what seat count?** | Distinguishes a revenue event from a logo event. The two require different investor framing (§12.4) |
| **Where did they go?** Competitor / third-party support / version freeze / in-house | Version freeze is recoverable over 3–5 years; competitor migration usually is not. Third-party support tells us our support-sunset schedule is the exposed flank (§6.5) |
| **What notice was given on support entitlements?** | The variable we most suspect [J]. If notice was under 12 months, our 36/48-month schedule is our principal differentiator |
| **Was there any price-certainty commitment?** | If not, this is where we buy consent most cheaply (§6.2) |
| **Was the price increase concurrent with the model change?** | Combining a model change with a price rise merges two conversations and loses both [J]. We recommend explicit separation (§7.5) |

### 2.2 Our working hypothesis

Our hypothesis — marked as such — is that the comparator combined (a) a short support-sunset notice, (b) no price-certainty window, (c) a de facto price increase presented as a model change, and (d) a sales force still paid on upfront value, which meant the field quietly advised its best accounts to buy perpetual before the door closed and then had no relationship credit left when it did [J]. Each of those four is separately avoidable. §§6, 7 and 9 avoid them in that order.

### 2.3 The asymmetry test — to be run before Board approval of pace

For each decile of the installed base by ARR, we compute:

**Value at risk (decile) = ARR(decile) × P(defection | scenario) × [multiple applied to recurring revenue] − ARR(decile) × conversion uplift × P(conversion) × [same multiple]**

The output is a single page: which deciles we should protect at almost any cost, which we should convert at standard terms, and which we should be willing to lose. We recommend the pace in §7 be set by the **top three deciles only**. Managing the transition to the average customer is how the average is achieved and the important customers are lost [J].

*Owner: CFO with Chief Customer Officer. Due: §15 item 1.*

---

## 3. Six assumptions in the existing model, respectfully tested

The model is well built and we have not duplicated it. We would ask that six inputs be re-examined; on three we believe the current setting is optimistic or pessimistic in a knowable direction.

| # | Assumption in the model [M] | Our view | Direction of error | Effect if we are right |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Conversion is voluntary and price-elastic, with a single blended conversion curve | Conversion behaviour is bimodal, not blended: large accounts convert on **budget cycle and audit exposure**, tail accounts on **price**. One curve averages two behaviours that need two offers | Understates achievable enterprise conversion; overstates tail conversion | Trough shallower but longer; enterprise incentives can be cheaper than modelled |
| 2 | 100% of on-premise subscription revenue recognised ratably | Term-licence structures allow a material portion at delivery, subject to auditor pre-clearance | **Materially overstates trough depth** | Directionally, the largest single correction available (§4.3) |
| 3 | Maintenance attrition continues at the historic base rate | Attrition **rises** during any announced transition, in every comparator we can see [P] | Understates trough depth | Partly offsets #2; the two should be modelled together, not separately |
| 4 | Sales productivity constant through the change | Productivity falls for 2–4 quarter…[truncated]

# Industrial Services Unit — Turnaround-or-Exit Assessment and Plan
## Diagnosis, Twelve-Month Plan, Exit Alternatives and Decision Architecture

**Version 2.0 — complete for decision. For the Board Strategy & Investment Committee. Circulated in advance to the ISU Managing Director and leadership team, Group CFO, Group General Counsel, Group HR Director and the four divisional MDs whose accounts are affected by §6. Not yet for customer, employee, works-council or market communication (§13).**

---

### How to read this pack

Three notes, then the substance.

**On what this is not.** It is not a third restructuring proposal. Two have been attempted; both delivered cost reduction and neither closed the loss [F]. That is evidence, not misfortune, and §3 sets out what it is evidence *of*. This is not a criticism of the colleagues who executed those programmes — they did what was asked, and did it. It is a criticism of the question they were given.

**On numbers.** No verified financial data has been made available to us. Every figure in this pack is therefore either a named variable awaiting input, or an illustrative value used only to show how the arithmetic behaves. Illustrative values are marked *[illus.]* and carry no evidential weight. §3.6 is the data request schedule: source system, owner, delivery date. The Committee should refuse to argue about any number in this pack that is not sourced there.

**On dates.** The Board has given twelve months [F]. Twelve months is the deadline for *evidence*; it cannot also be the deadline for *decision*. A business sold in month twelve of a fourth loss-making year is sold badly, and a sale process *begun* in month twelve is a wind-down with a press release. We recommend a dual track from day one with the substantive gate at **Month 5** (§12), the twelve-month date preserved as the outer boundary, and earlier trapdoors (§10.7) that fire without waiting for the gate.

---

## 1. Recommendation on a page

**Run a genuine dual track. Build one fact base that serves both outcomes. Decide at Month 5 against a stated economic inequality, with operational criteria subordinate to it. Fix price and perimeter before attempting growth, and never shrink the perimeter without first mapping which fixed costs actually leave with it. Bind the centre — allocation, intercompany pricing and internal recruitment — because on the facts available the centre is inside the causal chain, and a plan that does not say so will fail for reasons no one writes down.**

| | |
|---|---|
| Diagnosis, headline | Cost-out has been delivered twice and absorbed twice. The loss is sustained by a four-term bridge in which **volume loss, price erosion, mix deterioration and fixed-cost under-absorption** interact; under-absorption is the term both prior programmes ignored, and it is why cost reduction larger than revenue decline still failed to close the gap (§3.2) [A][H] |
| Structural vs execution | **We decline to publish a split before the Month-2 fact base.** A split asserted now would be decoration. §3.3 gives the five tests that produce it and the classification into *execution-recoverable*, *structural-perimeter* (recoverable only by exiting) and *structural-permanent* |
| Primary risk, ranked 1 | **Demand.** The order book is shrinking [F]. That is share loss, price-led loss, customer in-sourcing, or end-market decline — §3.5 decomposes it. Any plan that treats the demand side as stable is not a plan |
| Primary risk, ranked 2 | **Capability drain.** Best managers transferring out, largely to sister divisions [F]. This is the risk turnarounds routinely under-manage, and it is partly self-inflicted by the Group (§7) |
| Primary risk, ranked 3 | **Going-concern doom loop.** Customers do not sign multi-year maintenance and inspection contracts with a supplier believed to be for sale. A visible dual track can accelerate the very decline it exists to arrest (§8) |
| Where profit plausibly is | Recurring maintenance on the installed base, regulated inspection and certification, spares/consumables attach, scheduled turnaround work — **only where route density and repricing rights exist** (§5.3) [H] |
| Where it plausibly is not | Staffed labour supply, capital installation, sub-density geographies, and legacy contracts without indexation. Group-linked accounts must be tested, not assumed (§5.4, §6) [H] |
| The shrink trap | Perimeter reduction is invalid without a **step-fixed-cost map** showing which costs leave, at what volume threshold, and what the remaining core must then carry (§4). Two prior programmes appear to have cut cost without moving this map |
| Centre's own obligation | Allocation freeze at Month 0; **arm's-length intercompany pricing with any concession charged to the benefiting division, not to ISU**; internal-transfer approval at Group CEO level plus transfer fee; 10-working-day board response standard (§9) |
| Cross-subsidy consequence, stated plainly | Repricing intercompany work **moves margin between divisions; Group cash is unchanged.** It makes ISU's P&L honest, not better. The Committee must accept this in writing or the turnaround will be a paper one (§6.3) |
| Decision rule | **Economic master rule** (§12.1): retain only if risk-adjusted NPV of turnaround, net of total cost-to-try and stranded cost, exceeds certain-equivalent net proceeds available now, plus quantified option value of retained customer access. Five operational gate criteria (§12.2) are *necessary but not sufficient* |
| Gate rule, unambiguous | **All five criteria must be met.** One 30-day cure, available once, on one named criterion, and only if the cash and retention criteria are both already met. Four-of-five is a fail (§12.3) |
| Exit alternatives | **Six, named and ranked in §11**: whole trade sale; sequential carve-out/break-up; sponsor platform sale; MBO/MBI with vendor support; JV/partial sale preserving Group customer access; managed run-off with contract novation |
| Total cost-to-try | Defined as an equation in §12.4: twelve months of operating loss + programme spend + restructuring cash + value decay of a delayed sale + stranded cost crystallised late. This single comparison is the reason the pack exists |
| Resourcing sought | Parameterised in §14.2. The one non-negotiable line is a **retention pool that pays on either outcome** — it is worthless as a retention instrument if it pays only on turnaround success |
| Decisions requested | **Four** — §14.5, sought on **24 April** |
| Ownership | ISU Managing Director accountable for the turnaround track. A **separate, ring-fenced exit-track lead reporting to the Group CFO**, appointed within 15 days. One person cannot credibly run both, and asking them to will produce a compromised version of each |

### 1.1 Confidence, and the honest posture

A business that has cut cost twice without moving its loss is telling you that its problem is priced into its revenue and its capacity, not into its cost line [J, supported by the structure at §3.2]. The trap it has walked into twice is ordinary: cost-out is measurable, board-legible and within management's unilateral control, so it is what gets proposed. Price realisation, bid discipline, contract structure and perimeter are none of those things, so they get deferred. The result is an organisation that becomes progressively better at delivering cheaply the work it should never have taken.

We should say plainly, since it will be thought in the room in any case: **on the facts available, exit is at least as likely to be right as turnaround.** This pack is not written to defend the unit. If the Month-2 fact base returns as we suspect it may on density and repricing rights, we will say so in Month 2 rather than Month 12, and the Committee should hold us to that.

We would also ask that exit be described, from the outset and consistently, as an honourable outcome rather than a defeat. If the organisation believes that only turnaround counts as success, the fact base will bend, the gate will be argued rather than measured, and the people who matter will leave before Month 5.

---

## 2. The prior question the Board has not yet answered

### 2.1 "A credible path to profitability" needs a number

The Board's instruction is clear in intent and undefined in measurement [F]. Left undefined, Month 12 becomes an argument about momentum and goodwill — an argument incumbent management wins by default and the shareholder loses. We ask the Committee to ratify a definition on 24 April.

| Test | Proposed threshold | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Run-rate profit | **EBIT ≥ 0 at the Month-12 exit run-rate**, on the perimeter *locked at Month 5*, before restructuring charges, after full arm's-length Group allocation | "Run-rate" prevents a flattering final quarter; "locked perimeter" prevents winning by redefinition; "full allocation" prevents winning by accounting |
| Cash quality | **EBIT-to-operating-cash conversion ≥ 70%**, with unbilled WIP days and contract-retention balances no worse than the Month-0 baseline | Services businesses can manufacture EBIT through WIP and percentage-of-completion recognition. Cash is the honest test |
| Trajectory | Contracted bridge to **ROCE ≥ Group WACC + 200bps within 24 months** of Month 12 | Breakeven is not an investment case. Zero is not a destination |
| Self-funding | **No incremental Group cash from Month 9**, within the approved envelope | Earliest reliable indicator; hardest to dress |
| Quality of the bridge | **≥70% of the identified bridge in signed, contracted or executed actions** — not pipeline, not plan | This is what distinguishes a turnaround from a forecast |
| Demand | **Rolling twelve-month book-to-bill ≥ 1.0 on the retained perimeter, split recurring vs project**, with recurring renewal rate ≥ target and realised-price-vs-target improving | Point-in-time book-to-bill in long-cycle contracting is lumpy; one renewal flatters it |

**Perimeter lock.** The perimeter is fixed by board resolution at Month 5 in a signed schedule naming contracts, branches, service lines and legal entities. Any subsequent change requires Committee approval and restates the baseline publicly. Without this, "EBIT ≥ 0 on the retained perimeter" is meaningless.

**A profitable shrinking business** — positive EBIT with book-to-bill persistently below 1.0 — is an orderly liquidation. That may be the right answer, but it should be called by its name and valued as such (§11, Option F).

---

## 3. Diagnosis: is this structural or execution?

### 3.1 What the two prior programmes tell us

Two restructurings reduced cost and did not reduce loss [F]. There are only four explanations, and they are not mutually exclusive:

1. **Savings were real but absorbed** by contribution lost to volume and price.
2. **Savings were partly notional** — announced gross, eroded by leakage, inflation, re-hiring, contractor substitution and one-off delivery costs.
3. **Cost left, capacity did not.** Headcount and SG&A were cut; depots, fleet, licences, bonding, QHSE infrastructure and IT remained. Volume fell against an unchanged step-fixed base, so **unit cost rose while total cost fell**.
4. **Mix worsened.** The work retained during decline was disproportionately the low-margin, price-competed work, because that is the work that is easiest to keep.

Explanation 3 is the one that reconciles the apparent paradox of "cost reduction larger than revenue decline, loss unchanged." It is also the one that neither prior programme was designed to address, and it is the reason a third cost programme would fail identically [J].

### 3.2 The bridge, as algebra rather than as assertion

We express the three-year deterioration as an identity so that the Committee can see which term is doing the work once real data arrives:

**EBIT₃ = EBIT₀ + (S·r) − (ΔV · cm) − ΔP − ΔM − U − R + ΔI − i**

## 1. The disqualifying issue: the document does not exist yet

The submission terminates mid-sentence at "**Evidence markers.** [F] f". What has been delivered is a title block, a distribution list and three framing notes — approximately 400 words of preamble in front of a pack that is claimed to run to at least §14.

- **Evidence-marker system is invoked and never defined** (the legend is the sentence that gets cut). [F] is used once, on the competitor fact, while the adjacent causal claim ("did not, we suspect, lose it on price") carries no marker and no support. Markers applied inconsistently are worse than no markers.
- **"The observable failure mode in this category is…"** is presented as empirical regularity with no case base. Adobe, Autodesk, PTC, Sage, Splunk, Ansys and Citrix are all public, documented transitions with disclosed trough shapes. Asserting a pattern while declining to cite the five companies that establish it is an avoidable own goal.

## 3. Method concern: imported voice, not adapted analysis

The pack is a close stylistic transfer from the ISU turnaround-or-exit assessment — the "three notes," the "on what this is not / on numbers," the "we would ask the Board to decline any argument about a number in this pack," the §-number promissory notes. The problem is that the two briefs demand opposite things:

- The ISU brief asked *should we keep this?* — evidentiary humility and a decision gate were the deliverable.
- This brief asks *design the transition* — offer, price, comp, comms. The Board has already decided the direction. Deferring every number to a future fact base does not produce a plan; it produces a request for more time. If the current draft's trajectory holds, §§3–14 will arrive as an algebra pack with a Month-5 gate, and the Board will still not know what to charge a perpetual customer.

The correct structure is **decision-first with parameters**: name the offer tiers, the migration ladder, the comp mechanics and the disclosure regime, then state which parameter values are pending and what data will set them. Design choices are largely insensitive to the exact numbers; only calibration is sensitive.

## 4. Substantive omissions signalled by the fragment

The framing shows no awareness of the mechanics that actually determine trough depth. A passing version must engage at minimum:

**Revenue recognition and trough shape.** The single largest lever is the choice between SaaS/hosted (fully ratable), on-premise **term licence** (a material portion recognised at delivery under ASC 606 / IFRS 15) and hybrid. A term-licence bridge can cut reported-revenue trough depth by half while still building recurring commitments. The pack mentions "revenue-recognition systems" as plumbing but shows no sign of treating rev-rec as a *design variable*. This is the biggest miss.

**Revenue trough vs cash trough.** These are different troughs with different remedies (annual-upfront billing, multi-year prepay discounts, deferred revenue and RPO build). Investors discount the two differently. Nothing here distinguishes them.

**The maintenance base is the real asset.** "Long-standing customers feel entitled to the licences they already bought" is, commercially, a fight about *maintenance and support entitlements*, not licences. Perpetual licences are irrevocable contract rights; support is renewable and sunsettable subject to notice terms. The whole migration economics problem is: what multiple of current maintenance does the subscription price sit at, what uplift cap and price-certainty window are offered, and what is the support-sunset schedule. None of this is anticipated.

**The competitor's 20% loss is the design constraint and is under-used.** The lesson is not "we suspect it wasn't price." The lesson is that *removing optionality abruptly* triggers defection to competitors, third-party support providers and version freeze. The correct response is a decomposition of the 20%: which segments left, at what ARR, and — critically — the asymmetry test. Losing 20% of seats at a 1.7× revenue-per-retained-customer uplift may be value-accretive; losing 20% of the *top decile* is not. The pack should size this before designing anything.

**Sales compensation mechanics.** Untouched, but the standard toolkit is known: multi-year ACV credit or TCV crediting with a transition multiplier, ratable quota retirement, a protected-earnings / guarantee period for two to four quarters, a transition bonus pool funded from the trough, clawback on early churn, and — the hard part — a quota-setting and territory redesign that survives the reps' first look at their new W-2 trajectory. Also absent: the **channel**. The distribution list names a Head of Partner/Channel (good instinct) but VAR margin economics collapse under subscription and partners will actively resist migration if their upfront margin is not replaced.

**Governance and ownership.** The ISU pack's strongest structural idea — a ring-fenced second track with its own lead and reporting line — has no analogue here. A transition needs a dual operating model: perpetual run-off and subscription new-business managed and reported separately, with a named Transition Office owner. Nothing in the fragment establishes who owns this.

**Investor architecture.** "Keeps investors and the board committed through the trough" requires specifics the pack does not foreshadow: the metric switch (ARR, cRPO, NRR, gross retention, cohort conversion rate, billings), whether to suspend or re-base guidance, a pre-published trough shape with committed floor and recovery quarters, an Analyst Day with cohort disclosure, non-GAAP bridge policy, buyback/balance-sheet buffering, debt covenant renegotiation *before* announcement, and index/shareholder-base rotation from value to growth holders. Also absent: the board's own incentive metrics and the Compensation Committee, without whose prior action the executive team is being asked to depress the metrics it is paid on.

## 5. Distribution list gaps

Present: CEO, CFO, CRO, CPO, GC, CAO, VP IR, Channel. Missing and material: **Compensation Committee chair** (executive and sales comp redesign), **Audit Committee chair** (rev-rec position and auditor pre-clearance), **Treasurer** (covenants, liquidity through trough), **Chief Customer Officer / Head of Renewals** (owner of the entitlement conversation), and **CIO/Head of Business Systems** (billing, CPQ, entitlement management — the stated long-lead constraint).

## 6. What is worth keeping

Three things in the fragment are genuinely good and should survive into v2:

1. **The Phase 0 argument** — that the longest-lead, least-urgent-feeling items (billing stack, auditor position, covenants, board metrics) must be moved first, and that "a transition announced before its plumbing exists announces its own failure on a nine-month delay." That is the correct organising insight and it is well expressed.
2. **The framing that this is not a pricing exercise with a comms annexe** — the multi-system alignment point is right and is where most of these transitions fail.
3. **The instinct to test rather than accept the competitor read-across**, and the discipline of a named data schedule with owner and date.

## 7. Minimum contents of a passing v2

Recommendation on a page (named offer tiers, named price ratios, named comp mechanics, named disclosure regime) → competitor-failure decomposition and the 20%-loss asymmetry test → offer architecture including hybrid term-licence option → migration ladder for existing licence holders (grandfathered support tier, trade-in credit for residual licence value, price-certainty window, uplift cap, loyalty pricing tied to early conversion, hard support-sunset dates with legal review) → pricing model showing the explicit trade curve between conversion rate and trough depth, with three scenarios → the four-way bridge (bookings → billings → revenue → cash) under each scenario → sales and channel compensation redesign with transition-period guarantees and quota mechanics → systems, rev-rec and covenant Phase 0 → investor and board communication plan with metric switch, pre-committed trough shape and re-acceleration proof points → governance, ownership, phasing and abort/adjust triggers.

**Overall Assessment: MAJOR_REVISIONS**

1. **The Phase 0 argument** — that the longest-lead, least-urgent-feeling items (billing stack, auditor position, covenants, board metrics) must be moved first, and that "a transition announced before its plumbing exists announces its own failure on a nine-month delay." That is the correct organising insight and it is well expressed.
2. **The framing that this is not a pricing exercise with a comms annexe** — the multi-system alignment point is right and is where most of these transitions fail.
3. **The instinct to test rather than accept the competitor read-across**, and the discipline of a named data schedule with owner and date.

## 7. Minimum contents of a passing v2

Recommendation on a page (named offer tiers, named price ratios, named comp mechanics, named disclosure regime) → competitor-failure decomposition and the 20%-loss asymmetry test → offer architecture including hybrid term-licence option → migration ladder for existing licence holders (grandfathered support tier, trade-in credit for residual licence value, price-certainty window, uplift cap, loyalty pricing tied to early conversion, hard support-sunset dates with legal review) → pricing model showing the explicit trade curve between conversion rate and trough depth, with three scenarios → the four-way bridge (bookings → billings → revenue → cash) under each scenario → sales and channel compensation redesign with transition-period guarantees and quota mechanics → systems, rev-rec and covenant Phase 0 → investor and board communication plan with metric switch, pre-committed trough shape and re-acceleration proof points → governance, ownership, phasing and abort/adjust triggers.

**Overall Assessment: MAJOR_REVISIONS**

# Business-Model Transition: Perpetual Licence to Subscription
## Offer Architecture, Migration Economics, Sales and Channel Compensation, Trough Governance

**Version 2.0 — complete for decision.** For the Board.
Circulated in advance to: CEO; CFO; **Treasurer**; Chief Revenue Officer; Chief Product Officer; **Chief Customer Officer / Head of Renewals**; General Counsel; Chief Accounting Officer; **CIO / Head of Business Systems (billing, CPQ, entitlement)**; VP Investor Relations; Head of Partner & Channel; **Chair, Compensation Committee**; **Chair, Audit Committee**.
Not yet for customer, employee, partner, analyst or market communication (§12.6, §14).

*Prior to Board circulation, the substance of §§6, 9 and 10 has been walked through individually with the CRO, the Head of Partner & Channel and the Chief Customer Officer, and the substance of §§4 and 11 with the CAO and Treasurer. Where their views differ from ours, we have recorded the difference rather than resolved it (§16.3). We would not wish the Board to discover a disagreement in the room that could have been surfaced on paper.*

---

### How to read this pack

Four notes, then the substance.

**On what this is not.** This is not a pricing exercise with a communications annexe attached. The documented failure pattern in this category is a company that redesigns its price book while leaving its compensation plan, its billing stack, its board scorecard and its investor narrative on the old model — and discovers six quarters later that every part of the organisation is still paid, measured and praised for selling the thing it has publicly stopped selling. Nor is it a request for more time. The direction has been decided by leadership [F]; our task is to specify it. Every design choice below is **named**; only the calibration is pending, and §15 says precisely which data sets it.

**On numbers, and on the existing model.** We have been shown leadership's transition model, which projects a multi-year revenue trough [F]. We regard it as soundly constructed and we have not rebuilt it. We would, respectfully, test six of its inputs (§3); on three we think the model is likely to be wrong, and we say in which direction. Beyond that model, illustrative values are used solely to show how the arithmetic behaves and are marked *[illus.]*. They carry no evidential weight and should not be quoted outside this room. Where a figure matters to a decision requested in §16, it appears in §15 with a named owner and a delivery date.

**On sequencing.** There is a natural instinct to defer the irreversible decisions until the reversible ones have been proved. It is a reasonable instinct and it is, we think, the trap. The longest-lead items — billing and entitlement systems, the auditor's revenue-recognition position, debt covenants, and the Board's own incentive metrics — are exactly the ones that feel least urgent and take longest to move. They sit in **Phase 0** (§11) for that reason. *A transition announced before its plumbing exists announces its own failure on a nine-month delay.*

**On consultation.** Two of the four constituencies affected by this plan — the field sales organisation and the long-standing installed base — will experience it as something being taken away. Our strong view is that neither should learn the shape of it from a company-wide announcement. §9.7 and §6.7 set out a deliberate sequence of small-group soundings, advisory-council testing and named-sponsor conversations *before* publication. This adds roughly five weeks to the calendar. We think it is the cheapest insurance in the pack, and it is the principal difference between our plan and what the comparator appears to have done (§2).

**Evidence markers.**
**[F]** fact stated in the brief. **[M]** figure or assumption drawn from leadership's existing transition model. **[P]** publicly documented comparator transition — directional only, to be verified by IR before any external use. **[A]** assumption, pending the data in §15. **[J]** our judgement, argued in the text and open to challenge.

## 1. Recommendation on a page

**Adopt a three-year "Balanced" transition. Do not force conversion; make staying more expensive than moving, slowly and predictably. Use an on-premise term licence as the deliberate trough-shaping instrument, not as a compromise. Price the entry conversion at parity with today's maintenance and buy the customer's consent with a three-year price-certainty window and a capped uplift thereafter. Pay the sales force on total contracted value with a declining transition multiplier and four quarters of protected earnings, and replace the channel's upfront margin before, not after, partners discover it has gone. Move the plumbing, the auditor position, the covenants and the Board's own comp metrics in Phase 0. Then pre-publish the trough — floor quarter, depth and recovery quarter — and be judged against a scorecard we choose, disclose and never quietly change.**

| | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| **Direction** | Subscription-first, but **not SaaS-only**. Three deployment forms sold from one price book: Cloud (ratable), **Term Licence on-premise** (partially recognised at delivery), Perpetual (closed to new customers at Month 12; available to existing base only by exception until Month 24) (§4, §5) |
| **The single largest trough lever** | Revenue recognition, treated as a **design variable, not plumbing.** Directing an [illus.] 35–45% of on-premise subscription bookings to term licence rather than hosted can materially reduce reported-revenue trough depth while building the same recurring commitment (§4.3) [J][A] |
| **Offer tiers** | Three editions — **Essential / Professional / Enterprise** — replacing the perpetual-plus-maintenance SKU sprawl. Enterprise carries the entitlements the top decile actually buys support for (§5.2) |
| **Headline price ratio** | Like-for-like Cloud subscription at **1.30–1.45 × current annual maintenance** for *new* customers; **1.00 × current maintenance for the first three years** for existing licence holders who convert in the Early Window (§6.2, §7.2) *[illus., calibrated by §15 items 3, 5, 9]* |
| **Migration ladder** | Four rungs, price rising and terms tightening at each: **Early Window (Months 1–12) → Standard Window (13–24) → Late Window (25–36) → Support Sunset.** No retrospective removal of perpetual rights, ever (§6) |
| **Trade-in credit** | Residual-value credit on the customer's declining unamortised licence value, applied against first-year subscription, capped and expiring with the Early Window (§6.3) |
| **The entitlement principle, stated plainly** | Perpetual licences are irrevocable property and we will say so publicly and without qualification. **Support, updates and cloud services are renewable and, with notice, sunsettable.** That distinction is the whole of the migration economics and must be handled as a relationship matter before it is a contract matter (§6.1) |
| **Support sunset** | Announced at Month 0, effective **Month 36** for new-version entitlement and **Month 48** for security-only support, with a priced Extended Support tier at 1.5× legacy maintenance for those who genuinely cannot move. Contractual notice periods verified per-contract by GC before announcement (§6.5) |
| **Sales compensation** | **TCV crediting with a transition multiplier declining 1.6× → 1.3× → 1.0× over three years**; ratable quota retirement; **four quarters of protected earnings at 90% of trailing-eight-quarter average**; migration-specific SPIFF; 12-month churn clawback; quota and territory reset published only after the soundings in §9.7 (§9) |
| **Channel** | Upfront VAR margin is structurally destroyed by subscription and partners will resist accordingly [J]. Replace with a **front-loaded first-year margin (higher than the old licence margin in year 1), a declining renewal annuity margin, a migration bounty per converted seat, and deal-registration protection extended to renewals** (§10) |
| **Trough shape, recommended scenario** | Balanced: revenue trough floor in **Q6–Q7**, depth **[illus.] 11–14%** below the Month-0 run-rate, recovery to prior peak by **Q11–Q13**; cash trough shallower and earlier than the revenue trough because of annual-upfront billing (§7.4, §8) [M][A] |
| **The two troughs** | **Revenue trough and cash trough are different animals with different remedies.** Cash is managed with annual-upfront billing as default, multi-year prepay discounts, and RPO build; revenue is managed with mix (term licence) and pace. Investors discount them differently and we will disclose them separately (§8) |
| **Investor architecture** | Metric switch to **ARR, cRPO, gross and net retention, cohort conversion rate, billings**; guidance **re-based to a three-year framework, not suspended**; trough floor and recovery quarter **pre-committed and published**; Analyst Day at Month 3 with cohort disclosure; covenant amendment **completed before announcement**; buyback used as a floor, not a rescue (§12) |
| **Board's own metrics** | The Compensation Committee must re-cut executive metrics **before** the announcement. We are otherwise asking the executive team to depress, deliberately and for three years, the numbers on which it is paid. This is a Phase 0 item, not a year-end item (§11.5) |
| **Governance** | **Dual operating model.** Perpetual run-off and subscription new business managed, forecast and reported separately, with a named **Transition Office** lead reporting to the CEO and dotted to the CFO, appointed within 15 days. The CRO cannot both hit this year's licence number and dismantle it [J] (§13) |
| **Adjust triggers, not abort triggers** | We do not recommend an abort trigger; a publicly reversed transition is worse than either state. We recommend **three pace-adjustment triggers** on gross retention, top-decile conversion and cash (§14.3) |
| **Decisions requested** | **Six**, listed in §16, sought at the Board meeting on **[date]** |

### 1.1 Our posture, said once and plainly

Two things deserve saying before the detail.

First: **the comparator's loss of a fifth of its installed base is the most valuable piece of information we have** [F], and it is the design constraint for everything that follows. Our reading — offered for testing, not for adoption — is that abrupt transitions do not fail on price. They fail because **optionality is withdrawn without notice**, which converts a pricing conversation into a dignity conversation, and dignity conversations are lost by vendors. A customer who is told "your choice is gone" will look at competitors, third-party support providers and version-freeze even when the economics of staying are better. §2 sets out how to size this before we design against it.

Second: **20% base loss is not automatically a failure, and 0% base loss is not automatically a success.** The relevant test is asymmetric (§2.3). Losing a fifth of the *seat* count at a materially higher revenue per retained customer may be value-accretive. Losing a fifth of the *top decile* — the reference customers, the multi-site accounts, the ones whose logos carry the analyst narrative — is not recoverable in this decade. We therefore recommend that the plan be tuned to protect the top decile almost regardless of cost, and be considerably more relaxed about the long tail, where a partner-led or self-serve motion may serve better than we do.

We would also ask that the transition be described internally, consistently and from the first day, as something the company is doing **with** its customers and its sales force rather than **to** them. If people believe otherwise, we will spend the trough managing defections rather than conversions, and the pace-adjustment triggers in §14.3 will all fire at once.

---

## 2. The comparator's 20%: decomposition before design

### 2.1 What we need to know, and how to know it

We should not design against a headline. Before the Month-3 gate we should decompose the comparator's loss from public sources and channel intelligence [P], accepting that the picture will be partial.

| Question | Why it changes our design |
|---|---|
| **Which segments left?** Small/tail, mid-market, or enterprise? | If tail-heavy, our tail can be moved to a partner-led motion and our own risk is lower than the headline. If enterprise-heavy, the Early Window incentives in §6.2 must be materially richer |
| **What ARR left, versus what seat count?** | Distinguishes a revenue event from a logo event. The two require different investor framing (§12.4) |
| **Where did they go?** Competitor / third-party support / version freeze / in-house | Version freeze is recoverable over 3–5 years; competitor migration usually is not. Third-party support tells us our support-sunset schedule is the exposed flank (§6.5) |
| **What notice was given on support entitlements?** | The variable we most suspect [J]. If notice was under 12 months, our 36/48-month schedule is our principal differentiator |
| **Was there any price-certainty commitment?** | If not, this is where we buy consent most cheaply (§6.2) |
| **Was the price increase concurrent with the model change?** | Combining a model change with a price rise merges two conversations and loses both [J]. We recommend explicit separation (§7.5) |

### 2.2 Our working hypothesis

Our hypothesis — marked as such — is that the comparator combined (a) a short support-sunset notice, (b) no price-certainty window, (c) a de facto price increase presented as a model change, and (d) a sales force still paid on upfront value, which meant the field quietly advised its best accounts to buy perpetual before the door closed and then had no relationship credit left when it did [J]. Each of those four is separately avoidable. §§6, 7 and 9 avoid them in that order.

### 2.3 The asymmetry test — to be run before Board approval of pace

For each decile of the installed base by ARR, we compute:

**Value at risk (decile) = ARR(decile) × P(defection | scenario) × [multiple applied to recurring revenue] − ARR(decile) × conversion uplift × P(conversion) × [same multiple]**

The output is a single page: which deciles we should protect at almost any cost, which we should convert at standard terms, and which we should be willing to lose. We recommend the pace in §7 be set by the **top three deciles only**. Managing the transition to the average customer is how the average is achieved and the important customers are lost [J].

*Owner: CFO with Chief Customer Officer. Due: §15 item 1.*

## 3. Six assumptions in the existing model, respectfully tested

The model is well built and we have not duplicated it. We would ask that six inputs be re-examined; on three we believe the current setting is optimistic or pessimistic in a knowable direction.

| # | Assumption in the model [M] | Our view | Direction of error | Effect if we are right |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Conversion is voluntary and price-elastic, with a single blended conversion curve | Conversion behaviour is bimodal, not blended: large accounts convert on **budget cycle and audit exposure**, tail accounts on **price**. One curve averages two behaviours that need two offers | Understates achievable enterprise conversion; overstates tail conversion | Trough shallower but longer; enterprise incentives can be cheaper than modelled |
| 2 | 100% of on-premise subscription revenue recognised ratably | Term-licence structures allow a material portion at delivery, subject to auditor pre-clearance | **Materially overstates trough depth** | Directionally, the largest single correction available (§4.3) |
| 3 | Maintenance attrition continues at the historic base rate | Attrition **rises** during any announced transition, in every comparator we can see [P] | Understates trough depth | Partly offsets #2; the two should be modelled together, not separately |
| 4 | Sales productivity constant through the change | Productivity falls for 2–4 quarters through comp change, quota reset and a new selling motion [P][J] | Understates trough depth and length | Argues for the protected-earnings period in §9.3 as a cost of the plan, not a concession |
| 5 | Services revenue unaffected | Subscription reduces large implementation events and shifts services toward adoption and success work at different margin | Overstates services revenue, understates services margin change | Second-order but visible to analysts, who will ask |
| 6 | Cash follows revenue | Cash follows **billings**, and annual-upfront billing decouples the two | **Overstates the cash trough** | Materially eases the covenant and liquidity conversation (§8, §11.4) |

**Recommended action:** a single reconciled model, owned by the CFO, with these six inputs re-set and each labelled with its evidence source. We would ask that the Board be shown *one* model. Two models circulating is how a transition acquires two factions.

---

## 4. Revenue recognition as a design variable

### 4.1 Why this belongs in the offer section, not the accounting section

The trough is a *reported-revenue* phenomenon. The recurring-commitment build is an *economic* phenomenon. They are not the same, and the wedge between them is revenue recognition. Treating rev-rec as plumbing surrenders the single largest lever on the number investors will actually see [J].

### 4.2 The three forms

| Form | Recognition, directionally | Customer appeal | Trough effect | Strategic cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Cloud / hosted subscription** | Ratable over term | High for new, mid-market, greenfield | Deepest trough | None strategically — it is the destination |
| **Term licence, on-premise** | Licence element at delivery, support/updates ratable, subject to distinct-performance-obligation analysis under ASC 606
